instagram_caption:
What if the internet switched off for one hour? 🌐

At 12:00, every connection drops. Maps, chats, card machines and flight boards all go quiet. In a normal hour the world sends and receives about 16 billion emails (Radicati's 2026 forecast is about 392 billion a day), and Visa alone handles about 30 million payments (257.5 billion in fiscal 2025, averaged).

Here's the twist: the internet isn't in the sky. About 99% of the data crossing oceans travels through cables on the seabed. TeleGeography counts about 570 in service, and for most of the way across the ocean they're about as thick as a garden hose.

It has happened, a little. On 4 October 2021, a routine maintenance command accidentally cut Meta's data centres off from the internet, and Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp vanished for about six hours. On 19 July 2024, one faulty CrowdStrike update crashed about 8.5 million Windows PCs (Microsoft's estimate), and more than 4,000 flights were cancelled that day (Cirium).

This is fiction. The cables are real.

Did you spot him? 👀
